record.narrative: This is the first exploration pass, so I register a broad but pre-specified set of 12 binary biomarker/covariate contrasts across 12 CRISPR dependency outcomes. Because predictor names are opaque, I avoid assuming clinical meaning and instead treat measured binary status or a known two-level categorical predictor as the exposure. This supports scientifically falsifiable statements while remaining conservative about interpretation. Dependency scores are oriented such that more negative values mean stronger dependency. Therefore, a raw exposed-minus-comparator mean difference <0 corresponds to stronger dependency in the exposed group; I encode that as claim direction -1. Two contrasting hypotheses encode the alternative biology where a measured marker might indicate redundancy, resistance, or reduced pathway dependence, yielding a less negative score; these use direction +1. I selected complete binary predictors with prevalences far from 0 or 1 so that both comparison cells exceed 20 observations. I included higher-variance and distinctive outcomes such as outcome_001, outcome_006, and outcome_014 to increase sensitivity to meaningful shifts, while also surveying several more conventional dependency outcomes. For these negative-mean outcomes, the 10% clinical-significance threshold is roughly 0.009-0.042 score units depending on the outcome mean, so intervals and effect magnitude will be judged against that practical scale. All claims are initially unresolved.

No claims have evidence yet, and assessments_due is empty. To populate the discovery ledger, I will run all 12 registered first-pass comparisons now. They are mutually independent mean-difference screens over complete binary or two-level categorical predictors, with adequate cell sizes. This maximizes information from the initial analysis budget while preserving the pre-registered directions and practical threshold for subsequent appraisal.

I assessed all 12 discovery comparisons against a 10% practically important threshold using the absolute value of each outcome's population mean, since the dependency scores are negative. None of the original claims has sufficient evidence for a clinically meaningful association in its pre-registered direction. The only original-direction candidate is H7: feature_050=1 versus 0 for outcome_002 has signed estimate +0.0151, with 95% Welch interval [-0.0039, +0.0342]. The clinical threshold is approximately 0.0260, so the interval is compatible with a meaningful stronger-dependency effect, but the interval also includes null and a small opposite effect, and the point estimate is below the clinical threshold. I therefore leave H7 unresolved and keep it active rather than accept it. I request independent validation for H7 because it is the most direct borderline candidate and validation could clarify whether feature_050's apparent association is real or discovery noise. Several claims can be rejected for the pre-registered clinically important effect because the direction-aligned upper confidence bound is below the 10% threshold, or the entire interval lies within a non-clinical range. These include H1, H2, H4, H5, H6, H8, H9, H11, and H12. Two claims, H3 and H10, remain unresolved but closed for now because their confidence intervals are wide enough to include clinically meaningful effects while the point estimates are small; they do not justify follow-up before more targeted evidence arrives. H2 and H5 are notable because their point estimates point opposite to the original claims. For H2, outcome_006 and feature_002=1 versus 0 are more negative than expected by the original direction, suggesting potentially stronger dependency. For H5, outcome_005 and feature_021=1 versus 0 are less negative, suggesting potentially weaker dependency. Because these are post-hoc reversals rather than confirmations of the registered claims, I reject the original H2 and H5 directions and register new opposite-direction refinement claims. These new proposals remain unresolved until independently analyzed; they are not accepted from the same discovery data alone.

The independent validation for H7 provides little support for a clinically important association between feature_050 and outcome_002. For outcome_002, whose population mean is -0.2597, a 10% clinically significant difference corresponds to roughly a 0.026-unit shift. With H7 direction -1, positive signed estimates indicate stronger dependency in the exposed group. Discovery R7 gave a signed mean_difference of 0.0151 [95% CI: -0.0039 to 0.0342]. Validation R13 gave a much smaller estimate, 0.0044, with an independent interval [-0.0252, 0.0340]. The validation point estimate is far below the 10% threshold and includes no net evidence of stronger dependency; nevertheless, its upper bound still allows a clinically important effect because the exposed cell is only 371. I therefore do not accept H7. Since the candidate did not replicate and additional follow-up on this exact pair would probably be low-yield, I leave H7 unresolved as a matter of evidentiary certainty but close it for this investigation cycle.

Across round 1, no claim can be accepted. Most discovery contrasts were either opposite to the registered direction or too small to justify a clinically meaningful association. H1, H4, H6, H8, H9, H11, and H12 are rejected for the pre-registered clinical effect because their practical significance bounds do not support a difference of at least 10% of the absolute outcome mean in the claimed direction. H2 and H5 were rejected for their originally registered directions because their observed raw contrasts were reversed, producing the new unresolved reversal claims H13 and H14. H13 is a modest, imprecise candidate for stronger outcome_006 dependency with feature_002=1; H14 is a modest candidate for weaker outcome_005 dependency with feature_021=1, with the signed interval excluding null but not the 10% clinical threshold. These reversal claims remain the best current leads, but they have not yet shown evidence of clinically meaningful effects and require independent confirmatory testing if available at the next appraisal. H3 and H10 remain unresolved but closed because their point estimates are small despite intervals that are wide enough to leave practical significance uncertain.

The scientifically appropriate conclusion from the supplied dataset is currently negative or inconclusive, not a list of supported predictors. No association should be interpreted causally or generalized to other cohorts based on these data alone. The most informative next analyses are independent validation of H14 and H13 if validation can be requested at the next appraisal, plus continuation of first-pass screening with complete, adequately sized binary predictors on outcomes and predictors not yet covered. I registered a balanced batch of 12 new mean-difference screens covering the four outcomes not yet examined (outcome_003, outcome_008, outcome_009, and outcome_011) and alternative predictors for outcomes with high variance or remaining uncertainty. This keeps the strategy pre-specified, broadens coverage, and reserves validation budget for any signal that emerges with a clinically plausible magnitude.

The most useful next step is to develop the two unresolved leads rather than simply add more undirected screens. H13 (outcome_006, feature_002=1 versus 0, claim direction -1) has a signed discovery estimate of 0.0209, near the approximately 0.0175-unit clinical threshold, but its interval still includes null. H14 (outcome_005, feature_021=1 versus 0, claim direction +1) has a signed estimate of 0.0201, near the approximately 0.0250-unit threshold, with an interval that excludes null but does not reliably exclude a nonclinical effect. I therefore register subgroup and interaction refinements using the complete, balanced binary marker feature_034. For H13, direction -1 means the hypothesis is that exposure to feature_002=1 produces a more negative raw contrast, i.e., stronger dependency, and that a negative interaction raw effect would indicate concentration of that stronger-dependency association in the feature_034=1 stratum relative to its complement. Anticipated modification direction is left uncertain (0) because the plausible alternatives are no heterogeneity or the opposite direction; the subgroup mean_difference refinement more directly states the extension of the H13 hypothesis within feature_034=1. For H14, direction +1 means the hypothesis is that feature_021=1 produces a less negative raw contrast, i.e., weaker dependency, and that a positive interaction would indicate concentration of this weaker-dependency association in feature_034=1. Again, the interaction modification direction is uncertain, while the subgroup mean_difference is a direct within-stratum test of the H14 lead. These refinements must be assessed separately from their parents; even a strong subgroup estimate would not by itself establish generalizability or causality.

I also register three new population-level screens to close the current outcome coverage gap: outcome_002, outcome_004, and outcome_010 have no active untested predictor screen after their earlier closed results. I choose feature_020 for outcome_002, feature_065 for outcome_004, and feature_045 for outcome_010, all exposed=1 versus 0 with complete data and adequately sized cells. The pre-specified direction -1 encodes the hypothesis that the exposed marker is associated with more negative dependency scores, i.e., stronger dependency. The plausible alternatives are no meaningful association or a protective/redundancy-like association with less negative scores. These are falsifiable but not biologically interpreted because predictor labels are opaque.

No new assessment is due. H13 and H14 remain unresolved and active. In the next appraise, if one of these leads or a new subgroup estimate provides a clinically plausible magnitude, validation should be requested for the single comparison most likely to resolve practical importance. The primary validation candidate remains H14 because it has a direction-aligned interval excluding null; if a new subgroup/interaction result is much stronger, that result should be considered instead.

I will run 12 new comparisons that maximize information without wasting the analysis budget on claims that already have evidence. First, I prioritize the four refinements tied to the two best current leads. H27-H28 ask whether the unresolved H13 association between outcome_006 and feature_002=1 versus 0 is concentrated in, absent in, or reversed within the feature_034=1 stratum. H29-H30 do the same for the unresolved H14 association between outcome_005 and feature_021=1 versus 0. The interaction claims test effect modification directly; the subgroup mean_difference claims provide the more directly interpretable within-stratum effect. These are the most valuable follow-ups because H13 has a clinically plausible point estimate but an imprecise interval including null, while H14 has a direction-aligned interval excluding null but a point estimate near rather than clearly above the 10% threshold.

I also run H31-H33 to complete population-level coverage for outcome_002, outcome_004, and outcome_010 with complete binary predictors. Their pre-specified direction is -1, so a positive signed estimate would indicate stronger dependency in the exposed group. These are independent broad screens rather than post-hoc follow-ups to a specific lead.

Finally, I select the five highest-information untested broad screens: H15-H19. They cover outcome_009, outcome_008, outcome_003, outcome_011, and outcome_001. Several have larger outcome variance or less prior coverage than other registered comparisons, so they offer useful discovery value. I do not rerun H13 or H14 because doing so would reuse the same evidence and add no information. After these results arrive, I will assess all new discovery estimates against the 10% practical-significance threshold and decide whether one comparison—most likely a clinically strong subgroup refinement or the original H14 lead—merges as the best candidate for the next voluntary validation request.

I assessed all new discovery evidence against a 10% practically important relative difference, using the absolute population mean of each outcome as the denominator because dependency scores are negative. Signed estimates are already oriented to the claim direction, so positive values support the claim and negative values point away from it.

The strongest current result is H30: within the feature_034=1 subgroup, outcome_005 is higher/less negative for feature_021=1 versus 0, with signed estimate 0.0294 and 95% interval [0.0037, 0.0551]. The clinical threshold for outcome_005 is approximately 0.0250. The point estimate exceeds this threshold, and the interval is entirely in the claimed direction, but its lower bound is below the practical threshold. Therefore H30 is not acceptable yet, but it is the best candidate for independent validation because it combines a clinically plausible magnitude, direction consistency, and exclusion of the null at 95%. I request validation of H30.

The corresponding interaction test H29 is imprecise: signed estimate 0.0194 [-0.0185, 0.0573]. It is suggestive but cannot establish that the H14 lead is concentrated in feature_034=1 relative to its complement. H29 is left unresolved but closed because H30 provides a more interpretable direct within-subgroup test.

For the H13 lead, the subgroup refinement H28 shows almost no within-feature_034=1 association: signed estimate 0.0036 [-0.0444, 0.0516], and the interaction H27 is negative but wide: signed estimate -0.0359 [-0.1054, 0.0336]. These do not establish concentration of the H13 effect in feature_034=1; the H27 point estimate is actually opposite to the claimed direction, although its interval still includes clinically meaningful positive values. Because the intervals remain compatible with clinically meaningful effects in the claimed direction, I keep H27 and H28 unresolved but close them as direct follow-ups. The original H13 population-level association remains unresolved and active, but H30 is a more informative validation target than H13 given its direction-aligned interval and larger relative point estimate.

The new population-level screens H31-H33 were null or opposite for their pre-specified stronger-dependency claims. H31 has upper bound 0.0243 versus threshold approximately 0.0260; H32 has upper bound 0.0215 versus threshold 0.0255; H33 has upper bound 0.0051 versus threshold 0.0252. In each case, even the direction-aligned confidence bound falls below the 10% clinical threshold, so these are rejected and closed.

The untested broad screens H15-H19 were also rejected and closed. Their upper practical bounds are below the 10% thresholds, or the point estimates are opposite to the pre-specified direction: H15 upper 0.0169 < 0.0256; H16 upper 0.0068 < 0.0282; H17 upper 0.0213 < 0.0253; H18 upper 0.0231 < 0.0301; H19 upper 0.0319 < 0.0415. None provides support for a clinically meaningful association in its registered direction.

The overall evidence remains exploratory. No predictor should be treated causally or generalizably at this stage. Feature names are opaque, and the H30 subgroup test was one of several pre-specified refinements, so multiplicity remains relevant. Independent validation of H30 is the most useful next step because a replicated interval that stays above null and ideally above the 0.0250 clinical threshold would materially change the assessment of feature_021 within the feature_034=1 stratum.

The independent validation of H30 does not support the original subgroup claim. H30 tested whether, among cells with feature_034=1, feature_021=1 versus 0 is associated with a higher/less-negative outcome_005 dependency score (claim direction +1; positive signed effects mean weaker dependency). Discovery R17 gave +0.0294 [95% CI: +0.0037 to +0.0551], but validation R26 gave -0.0151 [independent 0.0038 interval: -0.0563 to +0.0261]. The validation point estimate is opposite to the discovery estimate, includes the null, and is below the approximately 0.0250-unit 10% clinical threshold for outcome_005. Its upper bound (+0.0261) is only marginally above the threshold and is much less precise than the discovery interval. Taken together, the two independent datasets are inconsistent and do not establish a clinically meaningful feature_021 effect within the feature_034=1 stratum. I therefore keep H30 unresolved rather than reject absolutely, because the validation interval still includes some clinically important positive effects and the discovery interval was positive, but I close it because the failed replication makes further follow-up on this exact pair low-yield.

This failure reduces confidence in feature_021 as a clinically important predictor of outcome_005. H14 remains unresolved and active because it is a different, population-level claim and has direct discovery evidence with a positive signed interval, but its point estimate (+0.0201) is below the clinical threshold (+0.0250). The subgroup validation failure is not direct validation of H14, so I do not change H14's status; however, H14 should not be accepted unless independent validation shows an effect clearly exceeding the clinical threshold.

The overall research state remains: no claim is accepted; no predictor association should be interpreted causally or generalizably; predictor labels are opaque; and most tested contrasts are negative or too imprecise for practical significance. The current unresolved but clinically plausible lead is H13 (outcome_006 with feature_002=1 versus 0, direction -1): discovery estimate +0.0209, above the approximate 0.0175 clinical threshold but with an interval including null. Its direct feature_034 subgroup refinements did not clarify the effect: H28 was near null in feature_034=1 and H27 suggested possible concentration in the complement, albeit imprecisely. Therefore the next useful analysis is a direct complement-stratum test of H13 (proposed H34-equivalent proposal above). This will show whether the H13 population signal is carried outside feature_034=1 or is not localized to a subgroup.

I also propose a small set of broad follow-up screens using complete, high-frequency binary predictors with adequate cell sizes: outcome_006/feature_008, outcome_002/feature_047, outcome_014/feature_064, and outcome_011/feature_030. These complement the already registered active untested claims H20-H26. The next analysis stage should run H20-H26, the complement refinement for H13, and these high-prevalence screens, reserving at most one validation request for the single new comparison with the best combination of clinically plausible magnitude, pre-registered direction, and interval precision. If no new candidate exceeds the previous borderline evidence, the final conclusion should remain negative or inconclusive: the supplied dataset does not currently provide reliable evidence for a clinically meaningful predictor subgroup association among the tested comparisons.

There are no assessments due at this stage, so I am not changing any current accept/reject/unresolved judgments. The main scientific issue is still that the strongest lead, H13, is imprecise, while the best earlier subgroup candidate, H30, failed independent replication. To avoid chasing a failed subgroup pattern, I register a direct complement-stratum test for the parent H14 lead: outcome_005 with feature_021=1 versus 0 within feature_034=0, direction +1. This asks whether the original population-level H14 signal is carried by the complement stratum rather than by feature_034=1, where validation was inconsistent. This refinement is important because the feature_034=1 subgroup result had a strong discovery interval but opposite validation point estimate; if the complement stratum is stable and clinically sized, the parent population signal becomes more interpretable, whereas a null/complement opposite result would further weaken feature_021 as a useful predictor.

I also register high-prevalence complete binary screens to cover outcomes that currently lack active or plausible leads, especially outcome_001, outcome_003, outcome_004, outcome_009, and outcome_010. For outcome_001, which has a larger clinical threshold due to a larger absolute mean, I use feature_008 because it has the smallest comparator cell among the complete high-prevalence binary predictors but still has a large exposed cell, giving reasonable power. For outcomes with ordinary thresholds near 0.025, I use feature_023 or feature_030, both complete binary predictors with exposed prevalence near 0.88-0.90 and comparator counts around 200-250. The pre-specified direction -1 is the default hypothesis that the exposed marker is associated with a more negative dependency score, i.e., stronger dependency; the opposite direction remains a plausible alternative because predictor labels are opaque.

I add outcome_014/feature_050 direction -1 because outcome_014 has the smallest clinical threshold, approximately 0.0093, so even a modest raw negative shift can be practically important. feature_050 also produced a negative raw association in outcome_002 under H7, so testing it on outcome_014 is a targeted follow-up without assuming cross-outcome generalization. Finally, I add high-prevalence screens for outcome_007, outcome_016, and outcome_012 to reduce dependence on lower-prevalence active screens such as feature_006, feature_001, feature_046, and feature_052.

All new claims are registered as unresolved. The next analysis stage should prefer H34, the H14 complement refinement, the already registered high-prevalence screens H35-H38, and the most useful new outcome-coverage screens, especially outcome_014/feature_050 and outcome_001/feature_008. Low-prevalence active claims H20-H26 should be deferred unless analysis capacity remains after the higher-power candidates.

I am requesting the twelve most information-rich untested registered claims. H34 and H39 are prioritized because they directly localize the two active leads: whether the outcome_006/feature_002 signal is carried in the feature_034=0 complement (H34), and whether the population-level outcome_005/feature_021 association remains in the feature_034=0 complement after the failed validation of the feature_034=1 subgroup (H39). The remaining ten are high-prevalence or otherwise adequately sized population screens for outcomes that still need interpretable follow-up: outcome_006/feature_008, outcome_002/feature_047, outcome_014/feature_064, outcome_011/feature_030, outcome_001/feature_008, outcome_003/feature_023, outcome_004/feature_030, outcome_009/feature_023, outcome_010/feature_030, and outcome_014/feature_050. I include two outcome_014 screens because outcome_014 has the smallest 10% clinical threshold, making it scientifically important to test predictors with adequate power while remaining alert to the risk of detecting small but practically important shifts. I defer low-prevalence H20-H26 for now because H34-H45 are expected to give more stable interval estimates and cover more current leads. I do not rerun H13 or H14 because their direct evidence already exists; the subgroup refinements add the missing localization information. No evidence-based status changes are requested because no assessments are due at this stage.

I assessed the twelve newly delivered comparisons using the claim-specific 10% relative threshold, computed as 0.1*abs(population mean). Signed estimates are already oriented to the registered hypothesis direction: positive values support stronger dependency in the exposed group relative to the comparator, and negative values point away from the registered stronger-dependency claim.

H34 is the strongest new evidence. Within the feature_034=0 complement, outcome_006 with feature_002=1 versus 0 gives signed estimate +0.0395, which is about 2.25 times the clinical threshold of about +0.0175 for outcome_006. This also makes biological sense with the earlier null-like result in the feature_034=1 subgroup, H28 (+0.0036): the population-level H13 association may be carried mainly by the complement. The uncertainty remains large, however: the 95% interval is [-0.0108, +0.0898], so the interval includes the null and even modest opposite effects. Therefore H34 is not acceptable on discovery evidence alone, but it is the best candidate for independent validation among all available claims. I request validation of H34.

H35 gives another outcome_006 signal: feature_008=1 versus 0 has signed estimate +0.0178, just above the +0.0175 threshold, but the interval [-0.0333, +0.0689] is wide and imprecise. It does not establish a clinically meaningful effect and is secondary to H34. I leave it unresolved but deferred.

H36 is rejected and closed for outcome_002/feature_047. The signed estimate is essentially null and opposite (-0.0013), and the direction-aligned upper bound +0.0174 is below the clinical threshold of about +0.0260.

H37 and H45 are positive screens for outcome_014, the outcome with the smallest threshold, about +0.0093. H37, feature_064, gives +0.0122 with interval [-0.0277, +0.0522]; H45, feature_050, gives +0.0122 with interval [-0.0266, +0.0511]. Both point estimates exceed the very small clinical threshold, but both intervals are wide and include the null. Because outcome_014 was tested repeatedly in this batch, multiplicity and the small threshold mean these should be treated as exploratory secondary leads rather than acceptable findings. They are unresolved and deferred.

H38, outcome_011/feature_030, has a small positive signed estimate (+0.0031), far below the +0.0301 threshold, and a wide interval [-0.0351, +0.0413]. It cannot be accepted, but because the interval remains compatible with clinically important positive effects, I keep it unresolved and close it due to low priority.

H39 tests the feature_034=0 complement for outcome_005/feature_021, the parent H14 population lead. The signed estimate is only +0.0100 with interval [-0.0179, +0.0380], below the +0.0250 threshold. Together with the earlier failed validation of the feature_034=1 subgroup, this makes feature_021 much less promising for clinically meaningful effects. I keep H39 unresolved and closed because the interval still includes positive clinically plausible values, but it should not guide further follow-up.

H40, outcome_001/feature_008, gives a small opposite signed estimate (-0.0042) with a very wide interval [-0.0502, +0.0417]. The upper bound is barely above the large outcome_001 threshold of about +0.0415, so I do not reject absolute compatibility with a clinically meaningful positive effect, but the point estimate is opposite and the result is not useful. It is unresolved and closed.

H41, H42, H43, and H44 are rejected and closed. H41, H42, and H44 have negative/opposite point estimates and upper bounds below their clinical thresholds. H43 has a strong opposite point estimate (-0.0232) and a direction-aligned upper bound only +0.0023, well below the +0.0256 threshold for outcome_009; it does not support the registered stronger-dependency claim.

Overall, no claim should be accepted yet. The evidence remains dataset-specific, associational, and multiplicity-limited. H34 is now the single most informative candidate for independent validation because it combines a direction-aligned, above-threshold point estimate with a coherent subgroup localization relative to H13/H28.

No claim is currently supported by the accumulated evidence as a clinically meaningful predictor or subgroup association in this dataset. The due validations show that the strongest candidate did not replicate. H34 tested outcome_006 with feature_002=1 versus 0 within feature_034=0 under the stronger-dependency hypothesis. Discovery R27 gave signed effect +0.0395, about 22.5% of the absolute outcome_006 mean and well above the 10% threshold of about 0.0175, but independent validation R39 gave only +0.0072, about 4.1%, with interval [-0.0696, +0.0839]. The validation point estimate is below the clinical threshold, includes the null, and is inconsistent with the discovery magnitude. I therefore do not accept H34. I keep it unresolved but closed because the wide intervals still cannot formally exclude a clinically meaningful positive effect, while concluding that this subgroup localization is not a useful lead. This also weakens, but does not by itself kill, H13, the population outcome_006/feature_002 claim. H13 remains active because it is the only direct claim with a discovery point estimate above the threshold: R2 is +0.0209, about 11.9%, interval [-0.0139, +0.0556]. The subgroup failure suggests caution, but a population-level association could still replicate even if the feature_034=0 localization failed. H7 outcome_002/feature_050 validation R13 gives signed effect +0.0044, about 1.7%, after discovery R7 +0.0151, about 5.8%; both intervals include the null, and the validation upper bound remains above threshold. I keep H7 unresolved but closed: there is no support for a clinically meaningful effect, but absolute exclusion is not possible. H15 outcome_009/feature_042 was previously rejected because the discovery estimate was near null/opposite and its upper bound was below threshold. New validation R40 is also near null, signed +0.0019, about 0.7%, but its wide independent interval upper bound +0.0290 slightly crosses the threshold of about 0.0256. To remain consistent with uncertainty, I change H15 from reject to unresolved but closed; this is not support, only a refusal to claim absolute exclusion under the very wide validation interval. The overall pattern across H30, H7, H15, and H34 is that borderline discovery associations do not replicate. Earlier negative findings remain informative: many population screens were rejected because their direction-aligned upper bounds fell below the 10% threshold, and the feature_021/outcome_005 line is deprioritized after the failed H30 validation and weak H39 complement result. I therefore close H14 as unresolved but low yield. Secondary unresolved leads are H35 outcome_006/feature_008, H37 outcome_014/feature_064, and H45 outcome_014/feature_050, but each has wide uncertainty and multiplicity concerns. The most informative next analysis is validation of H13, the population outcome_006/feature_002 stronger-dependency claim. If validation yields an interval that excludes null and the point estimate remains above about 0.0175, that would support a dataset-specific population association; if validation is near null, opposite, or imprecise, the outcome_006/feature_002 line should be closed. In parallel, analysis should prioritize the untested high-prevalence coverage screens H46, H47, H48, H49, H50, H51, and H52, with lower-prevalence H20-H26 used only if capacity remains. All statements remain dataset-specific, associational, and noncausal; predictor labels are opaque, and multiple testing limits confidence.

No assessments are due, so I do not change any claim status in this explore stage. The current scientific situation is that no claim is accepted. The strongest remaining population-level lead is H13: outcome_006, feature_002=1 versus 0, hypothesis direction -1, with signed discovery estimate +0.0209, interval [-0.0139, +0.0556], and clinical threshold about +0.0175. The feature_034 localization was not convincing: H28 was near null in feature_034=1, and the feature_034=0 candidate H34 failed independent replication. Therefore I propose a different balanced effect-modifier localization for H13 using feature_060, because feature_060 is a complete binary variable with mean about 0.50 and should give reasonably powered subgroup comparisons. The two direct subgroup claims ask whether the outcome_006 feature_002 stronger-dependency association is present in the feature_060=1 stratum, the feature_060=0 stratum, both strata, neither stratum, or is opposite in one stratum. This is useful because a stable population effect would be expected to appear in both feature_060 strata if feature_060 is not a true modifier, whereas a large stratum-specific effect would support a subgroup claim and a null/opposite split would weaken H13.

I also propose a direct outcome_006/feature_060 main effect test with direction -1. If feature_060 itself is associated with substantially stronger dependency in outcome_006, this could become a clinically meaningful predictor; if it is near null or opposite, it reduces the plausibility that the H13 feature_002 signal reflects a broad dependency-related marker shared with feature_060.

For broader coverage, I register balanced binary feature_002 screens for outcomes where the 10% clinical threshold is large enough that a balanced comparison can provide informative interval precision: outcome_001, outcome_008, outcome_011, outcome_002, outcome_003, outcome_004, outcome_009, outcome_010, and outcome_012. feature_002 is chosen because it is the current positive lead in outcome_006 and because its prevalence is nearly balanced, giving better interval precision than the high-prevalence but small-comparator screens. The claim direction remains -1, representing the clinically meaningful hypothesis that feature_002=1 is associated with more negative dependency, i.e. stronger dependency. For these secondary outcomes I set anticipated_direction 0 because predictor labels are opaque and most prior screens have been null or imprecise; the plausible alternatives are null, opposite, or a genuine cross-outcome association. These screens can either identify a new clinically meaningful predictor or produce stronger negative closure than earlier high-prevalence comparisons.

The existing active high-prevalence screens H46 through H52 remain relevant, especially outcome_014/feature_002 H52, but the new feature_060 localization and balanced feature_002 screens should be prioritized for the next analysis because they combine better power with the most informative scientific hypotheses. If the feature_060 stratum results or future evidence strongly support H13, the next appraise stage should request validation of H13; if they are inconsistent or null, the outcome_006/feature_002 line should be deprioritized or closed. All proposed claims remain unresolved, associational, dataset-specific, and noncausal.

I will run the twelve most informative currently untested claims. First, H53 and H54 directly test whether the main remaining population-level lead, H13, is localized to the balanced feature_060=1 or feature_060=0 stratum. Because the previous feature_034 localization was inconsistent and the feature_034=0 candidate failed independent replication, these two stratum tests are the cleanest way to decide whether H13 remains a plausible clinically meaningful population association or should be deprioritized/closed. H55 tests feature_060 itself as a direct outcome_006 predictor and also helps interpret whether the H13 feature_002 signal is independent of a feature_060 main effect. Second, H52 tests outcome_014 under feature_002, the current lead predictor, using a balanced predictor with very small 10% clinical threshold; it can either add evidence that feature_002 is not merely outcome_006-specific or provide an additional null/contrary closure. Third, I run the balanced feature_002 cross-outcome screens H56-H63. feature_002 is nearly balanced and therefore should produce more precise intervals than many high-prevalence, small-comparator screens already tested. Testing feature_002 across outcome_001, outcome_008, outcome_011, outcome_002, outcome_003, outcome_004, outcome_009, and outcome_010 asks whether the H13 association has any coherent cross-outcome pattern in this dataset. I defer H64 and the other high-prevalence active screens H46-H51 for now because the feature_060 localization of H13 and the feature_002 cross-outcome screens are more tightly connected to the only current positive lead. No assessments are requested because no validations or new results are due in this analyze stage.

I assessed all newly delivered discovery results using the outcome-specific 10% relative clinical threshold, computed as 0.1 times the absolute population mean. Positive signed estimates support the registered stronger-dependency hypothesis because the outcomes are dependency scores with more negative values indicating stronger dependency.

The most important new evidence concerns outcome_006. Its clinical threshold is about +0.0175. H53 tests outcome_006, feature_002=1 versus 0 within the feature_060=1 stratum under the stronger-dependency hypothesis. R41 gives a signed estimate +0.0256, above the threshold, but the interval [-0.0232, +0.0744] includes the null and does not have a lower bound above the clinical threshold. Therefore H53 cannot be accepted, but it is the most informative subgroup result because it is direction-aligned and above threshold. H54 tests the feature_060=0 complement. R42 gives +0.0158, slightly below the threshold, with interval [-0.0336, +0.0653]. It does not establish a clinically meaningful subgroup effect, but it is same-signed and reasonably consistent with H53. This is useful because the earlier feature_034 localization was weak and H34 failed validation; by contrast, the feature_060 strata are both positive, making a stable population-level feature_002 association more plausible rather than an isolated subgroup artifact. However, both subgroup intervals are wide, so neither H53 nor H54 supports acceptance on discovery evidence alone.

H55 tests outcome_006, feature_060=1 versus 0 directly. R43 gives +0.0194, above the outcome_006 threshold, but interval [-0.0153, +0.0541] includes the null. It cannot be accepted and is not the primary lead. It is kept unresolved but deferred because it is a competing explanatory predictor: if feature_060 were strongly associated with outcome_006 and correlated with feature_002, it could contribute to the H13 signal. The fact that feature_002 contrasts are positive in both feature_060 strata argues against feature_060 completely explaining the signal, but it does not formally establish independence. Given limited validation capacity, I do not prioritize validating H55 over H13.

H13 remains the main unresolved population-level lead. Its original discovery estimate R2 is +0.0209 for outcome_006 feature_002=1 versus 0, about 11.9% of the absolute outcome mean, with interval [-0.0139, +0.0556]. The new feature_060 stratum results do not prove H13, but they provide coherent local support: both strata have positive signed estimates, and one exceeds the threshold. This makes an independent validation of H13 the most informative next test. If H13 validation gives a direction-aligned estimate near or above about +0.0175 with an interval that excludes the null, that would support a dataset-specific associational claim. If validation is near null, opposite, or imprecise despite including clinically meaningful positive values, the outcome_006/feature_002 line should be closed or heavily deprioritized. I request validation of H13 rather than H53 because H13 has the larger comparison cells, narrower interval, and represents the primary population-level hypothesis; H53 is narrower and more exposed to subgroup multiplicity.

H52 tests outcome_014, feature_002=1 versus 0. Outcome_014 has a very small threshold of about +0.0093 because its population mean is near zero. R44 gives a small opposite estimate -0.00085 with interval [-0.0327, +0.0310]. The point estimate is essentially null and opposite, and it does not support the registered stronger-dependency hypothesis. Because the direction-aligned upper bound is above the small outcome_014 threshold, I do not claim absolute exclusion, so I keep H52 unresolved. However, given the near-null opposite point estimate, the small threshold, the multiplicity of feature_002 screens, and the lack of cross-outcome coherence, it is low yield and should be closed.

The balanced feature_002 cross-outcome screens generally do not support a broad clinically meaningful association for the current hypothesis. H56 outcome_001/feature_002 gives +0.0061 with interval [-0.0260, +0.0383]. The outcome_001 threshold is about +0.0415, and the interval upper bound is below that threshold, so H56 is rejected and closed. H57 outcome_008/feature_002 gives +0.0149 with interval [-0.0067, +0.0364]. The threshold is about +0.0282; the point is below threshold, and although the upper bound is compatible with a clinically meaningful positive effect, the result is imprecise and low priority. I keep H57 unresolved but closed. H58 outcome_011/feature_002 gives an opposite estimate -0.0126 and upper bound +0.0105, below the threshold of about +0.0301; H58 is rejected and closed. H59 outcome_002/feature_002 gives +0.0054 with upper bound +0.0208, below the threshold of about +0.0260; rejected and closed. H60 outcome_003/feature_002 gives +0.0037 with upper bound +0.0195, below the threshold of about +0.0253; rejected and closed. H61 outcome_004/feature_002 gives +0.0069 with upper bound +0.0228, below the threshold of about +0.0255; rejected and closed. H62 outcome_009/feature_002 gives an opposite estimate -0.0069 and upper bound +0.0089, below the threshold of about +0.0256; rejected and closed. H63 outcome_010/feature_002 gives an opposite estimate -0.0035 and upper bound +0.0127, below the threshold of about +0.0252; rejected and closed.

Overall, no new claim should be accepted because every clinically plausible positive result has an interval that includes the null and does not demonstrate an effect size reliably above the relevant 10% threshold. The best next action is independent validation of H13, the population-level outcome_006/feature_002 stronger-dependency hypothesis. All conclusions remain dataset-specific and associational; predictor labels are opaque, and multiplicity warrants caution.

No claim is supported as a clinically meaningful association in this dataset. The due validations close the two strongest remaining leads. For H13, the outcome_006 clinical threshold is about 0.1*abs(-0.17545)=0.0175. Discovery R2 gave signed +0.0209, interval [-0.0139,+0.0556], just above threshold but including the null. Independent validation R53 gave signed +0.00233, interval [-0.0485,+0.0531], only about 0.0133 of the clinical threshold and clearly not supportive. Although the wide validation interval cannot formally exclude a positive clinically meaningful effect, the discovery-subgroup-validation sequence for outcome_006 feature_002 is now inconsistent and not a useful lead. I therefore keep H13 unresolved to avoid overclaiming absolute exclusion, but close the investigation. Consequently, H53 and H54 are also closed as unresolved localizers: R41 is above threshold but interval includes the null, and R42 is below threshold; without a stable population-level lead, neither subgroup claim is worth further capacity. For H30, outcome_005 threshold is about 0.02496. Discovery R17 gave +0.0294 with interval [0.0037,+0.0551], but independent validation R26 gave -0.0151 with interval [-0.0563,+0.0261]. The validation point is opposite to the hypothesis, includes the null, and its upper bound is only just above threshold. I reassess H30 as unresolved but closed because the subgroup claim is not supported, while the independent interval still makes absolute exclusion overly strong. Overall, H30, H34, H13, H7, and H15 show a recurring pattern: borderline discovery associations do not replicate. Feature_021/outcome_005 is deprioritized, outcome_006 feature_034 and feature_060 localizations are uninformative, and outcome_006 feature_002 is closed as a priority line. The most informative next work is broad negative coverage with reasonably powered unregistered or untested comparisons. I will prioritize untested active H46-H51 and H64, plus new binary screens for feature_045, feature_050, feature_052, and feature_065 across outcomes where cell sizes are adequate and threshold-relative precision is useful. I defer lower-prevalence H20-H26 unless a specific new reason emerges. No validation should be requested until a new discovery has a point estimate clearly above the 10% threshold with a not-too-wide discovery interval. All conclusions remain dataset-specific, associational, and noncausal.

No claim is currently accepted, and the two strongest leads have failed independent replication: H13 outcome_006/feature_002 did not validate, and H30 outcome_005/feature_021 within feature_034=1 also did not validate. The feature_002 cross-outcome screens are therefore not worth pursuing, so I close H64 as a low-priority untested extension of that closed line. The remaining useful scientific question is whether unresolved outcome_006 markers such as feature_060 and feature_008 represent broader dependency-associated markers, and whether reasonably powered untested binary predictors have clinically meaningful associations elsewhere. I propose a focused feature_060 panel for outcome_015, outcome_003, and outcome_007 because feature_060 is balanced, gives well-powered cells, and is currently only a single wide interval in outcome_006. I also propose feature_008 cross-outcome screens for outcome_011, outcome_008, outcome_013, and outcome_005; outcome_006/feature_008 was just near the outcome_006 clinical threshold, although its interval was wide, so a consistent same-sign pattern in other outcomes would be informative while inconsistent or null results would further deprioritize it. Finally, I register additional main-effect screens for feature_037, feature_012, feature_027, and feature_045 on outcomes where comparator and exposed cells are adequate and the 10% thresholds are meaningful. All new claims use direction -1, meaning the exposed group is hypothesized to have stronger dependency, but anticipated direction is 0 because predictor labels are opaque and most prior screens have been null. I also defer H46-H50 because high-prevalence feature_023 and feature_030 comparisons are likely less informative than the registered better-powered binary screens and the focused feature_060/feature_008 follow-ups. No validation is requested now; validation should be reserved for a clear discovery with a point estimate above the relevant 10% threshold and a reasonably bounded interval. All interpretations remain dataset-specific, associational, and noncausal.

I will run the twelve most informative currently untested claims: H73-H84. This batch directly follows the current allocation plan. First, H73-H75 test whether feature_060 is associated with clinically meaningful stronger dependency in outcome_015, outcome_003, and outcome_007. feature_060 is balanced, so these main-effect tests should be reasonably well powered and provide useful negative coverage or candidate leads after the prior outcome_006 feature_060 result was positive but imprecise and not a validated lead. Second, H76-H79 test feature_008 across outcome_011, outcome_008, outcome_013, and outcome_005. The earlier outcome_006/feature_008 result was near the clinical threshold but very wide, so these cross-outcome screens can either identify a consistent pattern or further deprioritize feature_008 as a marker. Third, H80-H84 add diverse, adequately powered binary predictor screens for feature_037, feature_012, feature_027, and feature_045 on outcomes where prior related tests were null or rejected but additional outcomes remain untested. This gives broad negative coverage and avoids spending resources on the already failed outcome_006/feature_002 and outcome_005/feature_021 lines. No validation is requested now because no new discovery in this batch has yet been observed. No assessments are due or requested.

I assessed the 12 newly delivered discovery results against outcome-specific clinical thresholds computed as 0.1 times the absolute population mean. Because the outcomes are CRISPR dependency scores, a positive signed estimate supports the registered hypothesis that the exposed group has stronger dependency. For all outcome-specific thresholds here, that gives approximately +0.025 for outcome_015/003/007/005, +0.028 for outcome_008, +0.030 for outcome_011, +0.027 for outcome_013, and +0.026 for outcome_002.

H73 outcome_015/feature_060 is rejected and closed: R54 is opposite to the hypothesis (-0.0010), and the upper bound +0.0143 is below the +0.0250 clinical threshold. H74 outcome_003/feature_060 and H75 outcome_007/feature_060 are also rejected and closed: R55 +0.0050 and R56 +0.0039 are far below threshold, and their upper bounds +0.0208 and +0.0194 are below the relevant thresholds. Together these indicate that feature_060 is not a clinically meaningful predictor of stronger dependency in outcome_015, outcome_003, or outcome_007, and they weaken the earlier outcome_006 feature_060 lead.

The feature_008 cross-outcome screens are mostly null except for H77. H76 outcome_011/feature_008 is rejected and closed because R57 is opposite and the upper bound +0.0279 is below the +0.0301 threshold. H78 outcome_013/feature_008 is rejected and closed because R59 is opposite and its upper bound +0.0186 is below the +0.0269 threshold. H79 outcome_005/feature_008 is rejected and closed for practical scientific reasons: R60 is very small (+0.0025), interval includes the null, and although the upper bound +0.0250 is effectively at the +0.0250 threshold, the point estimate is only about 1% of the mean and the result is not a useful lead. I would not call this a formal exclusion, but it does not support accepting or further investigating this predictor for outcome_005.

H77 outcome_008/feature_008 is the strongest new discovery. R58 gives signed +0.0322, which is about 11.4% of the absolute outcome_008 mean and above the +0.0282 clinical threshold. The 95% Welch interval [+0.0028, +0.0617] excludes the null, which makes this more credible than earlier borderline positive findings. However, the interval lower bound is below the clinical threshold, the comparator cell is smaller than the exposed cell, and this is one of many screened predictors. Therefore I do not accept it yet. I request independent validation of H77 to determine whether the effect is replicable and whether the interval supports a clinically meaningful difference. If validation is near null or opposite, the feature_008 line should be deprioritized; if validation is positive and reasonably aligned with the threshold, H77 can be considered for acceptance.

The remaining binary screens mostly do not support clinically meaningful associations. H80 outcome_015/feature_037, H82 outcome_002/feature_027, and H83 outcome_011/feature_045 are rejected and closed because their point estimates are small or opposite and their upper bounds are below the relevant clinical thresholds. H81 outcome_013/feature_012 and H84 outcome_007/feature_045 are unresolved but closed because R62 +0.0186 and R65 +0.0137 are below threshold, intervals include the null, and although their upper bounds are compatible with clinically meaningful positive effects, they are too imprecise and multiplicity-exposed to pursue without a stronger reason. Overall, H77 is the only result worth validation; no claim should be accepted before that validation.

The newly available validation evidence does not support any clinically meaningful association. I used the same practical rule as before: because all outcomes are CRISPR dependency scores with negative means, the relevant clinical threshold is approximately 0.1 times the absolute population mean for the outcome. For H34 (outcome_006), the threshold is about +0.0175. The discovery R27 was signed positive at +0.0395 but had interval [-0.0108, +0.0898]; the independent validation R39 is only +0.0072, about 41% of the threshold, with interval [-0.0696, +0.0839]. This is a clear failure to replicate a clinically meaningful effect. I keep H34 unresolved because the validation interval cannot formally exclude a positive clinically meaningful effect, but I close it because the discovery-subgroup-validation pattern is not a useful lead. With H13 also nonreplicating and feature_060 panels null, the outcome_006 feature_002/feature_034/feature_060 localization line is now deprioritized.

For H15 (outcome_009), the threshold is about +0.0256. Discovery R21 was opposite to the hypothesis at -0.0022 and had upper bound +0.0169, already below the clinical threshold. Independent validation R40 was +0.0019, far below threshold, with a wide interval [-0.0252, +0.0290]. The combined evidence pattern supports a negative result for this specific predictor-outcome association: the initial comparison ruled out a clinically meaningful positive effect at conventional discovery precision, and validation did not rescue it. I reject H15 and close it. This does not mean a large effect is mathematically impossible under the conservative validation interval, but the overall evidence does not support accepting a clinically meaningful association.

For H77 (outcome_008), the threshold is about +0.0282. Discovery R58 was the most promising result of the last batch: signed +0.0322, above threshold, with 95% interval [+0.0028, +0.0617]. It excluded zero, but its lower bound was below the clinical threshold, so it could not establish a 10% meaningful difference. Independent validation R66 is +0.0046, only about 16% of the threshold, with interval [-0.0416, +0.0509]. The validation point estimate is clearly non-supportive, and the two independent estimates together give no useful indication of a stable clinically meaningful association. I do not accept H77. I keep it unresolved rather than reject because the validation interval cannot formally exclude a positive clinically meaningful effect, but I close the investigation. I also close related feature_008 leads H35 and H51, and close feature_060 outcome_006 H55, because feature_060 was not replicated across other outcomes and feature_008 failed the strongest validation check. The same logic deprioritizes low-yield deferred comparisons H37 and H45.

Overall, the supported conclusion at this stage is negative: no claim is accepted as a clinically meaningful association in this dataset. Many predictor-outcome comparisons are rejected because their discovery intervals exclude clinically meaningful positive effects, including feature_060 panels for outcome_015/003/007, feature_008 panels for outcome_011/013/005, and feature_037/027/045 screens. Several previously promising but nonreplicating leads are now closed or unresolved-closed: outcome_006 feature_002, outcome_005 feature_021 within feature_034=1, outcome_006 feature_002 within feature_034=0, outcome_009 feature_042, and outcome_008 feature_008. The recurring pattern is that borderline discovery effects above the 10% threshold but without intervals excluding sub-threshold effects have not replicated.

The most informative next work is broad negative coverage among untested moderately common binary predictors, not further validation of failed predictors. I register feature_042 outcome panels for outcome_005, outcome_006, outcome_012, outcome_015, outcome_016, and outcome_002, linked to the prior H15 feature_042 test as a same-predictor motivation. feature_042 has adequate prevalence and was only tested in one outcome so far. These should be considered alongside existing active untested claims involving feature_045, feature_050, feature_052, and feature_065. I would only consider future validation if a new discovery has a point estimate clearly above the outcome-specific 10% threshold and a reasonably bounded interval, ideally excluding zero or with a lower bound approaching the threshold. All conclusions remain dataset-specific, associational, and noncausal; predictor labels are opaque, and generalization beyond this supplied dataset remains unsupported.

There are currently no accepted claims, and the strongest prior candidates have failed validation or have been rejected by well-powered negative screens. The most informative next exploration is to move beyond binary predictors and test nominal multi-level categorical predictors that have not yet been examined. Several variables have multiple nominal levels with reasonably large non-dominant cell sizes, including feature_055, feature_063, feature_036, feature_028, feature_048, feature_009, and feature_019. If a non-dominant level defines a distinct biological or molecular group, comparing that level against the dominant level may reveal a clinically meaningful dependency association that a binary screen could miss.

I register pairwise mean-difference contrasts for these categorical predictors across outcomes with relatively stable dispersion, mostly avoiding outcome_006, outcome_014, and outcome_001 where residual variance is larger relative to the mean. All proposals use direction -1, so a positive signed result indicates stronger dependency in the exposed level relative to the comparator level. The anticipated direction is 0 because predictor labels are opaque and prior screens have produced few positive leads. These are hypothesis-generating association tests in this dataset, not causal or generalizable claims.

I do not request validation at this explore stage. Future validation should be reserved for a new discovery whose point estimate is above the outcome-specific 10% threshold and whose interval is reasonably tight or excludes sub-threshold effects.

I will request the twelve newly registered categorical predictor screens H91-H102 because they directly test the current hypothesis that non-dominant nominal levels may show stronger dependency relative to dominant levels. These predictors have not yet been examined, and several non-dominant levels are large enough for Welch comparison. This batch gives useful negative coverage if null and identifies candidate leads if any signed estimate exceeds the outcome-specific ~10% clinical threshold. I prioritize these over older low-prevalence binary screens and deprioritized feature panels because no current validated or accepted leads remain.

I assessed all 12 categorical screens using outcome-specific clinical thresholds of 0.1 times the absolute outcome mean, which are approximately +0.0248 to +0.0269 depending on the outcome. No comparison supports a clinically meaningful stronger dependency in the registered exposed nominal level. Formal rejects are justified when the signed 95% upper bound was below the relevant threshold: H93 R69 (+0.0062, upper +0.0161 vs threshold +0.0250), H94 R70 (-0.0133, upper +0.0036 vs +0.0256), H97 R73 (-0.0066, upper +0.0162 vs +0.0245), H99 R75 (-0.0168, upper +0.0168 vs +0.0253), and H100 R76 (-0.0291, upper -0.0093 vs +0.0256). The other positive estimates are below threshold and imprecise: H91, H92, H95, H96, H98, H101, and H102. I closed these as unresolved because intervals include the null and some upper bounds still permit a 10% effect, but none is promising enough for validation. H100 is scientifically interesting only in the opposite direction: the point estimate implies level_003 has stronger dependency than level_001 by about 0.0291, or 11.4% of the absolute mean, with a 95% interval after reversal of [+0.0093, +0.0489]. Because this is an incidental reversal from a multiple-screening exercise and the reversed lower bound is below the clinical threshold, I do not accept it and did not request validation of H100, whose original hypothesis is already excluded. I registered one reversed follow-up proposal for outcome_009 feature_048 level_003 versus level_001 to evaluate this opposite signal formally, but it remains hypothesis-generating, dataset-specific, associational, and noncausal.

I reassessed the two due outcome_006 validation results using the outcome-specific 10% clinical threshold, approximately +0.0175 for a signed stronger-dependency contrast. For H13, discovery R2 was initially promising at +0.0209 but its lower bound was negative; independent validation R53 collapsed to +0.0023, far below the threshold, with a wide interval [-0.0485, +0.0531]. For H55, discovery R43 was similar at +0.0194 but validation R79 collapsed to +0.0015, interval [-0.0506, +0.0536]. These are clear nonreplication patterns for two previously borderline outcome_006 leads. I keep both claims unresolved rather than formally rejected because the independent validation intervals still cannot mathematically exclude a clinically meaningful positive effect, but I keep both closed because the combined discovery-validation evidence gives no useful reason to spend further resources on these predictor-outcome lines.

No claim is accepted at this checkpoint. The active candidate is H103, outcome_009 feature_048 level_003 versus level_001, derived from the reversed direction of H100. It has a clinically relevant signed point estimate (+0.0291, threshold +0.0256) and excludes the null, but its lower bound (+0.0093) remains below the clinical threshold and it emerged from reverse screening. It therefore remains hypothesis-generating rather than accepted. The most informative next work is to test whether this feature_048 level_003-versus-level_001 signal replicates across stable adjacent dependency-score outcomes. I registered outcome_010, outcome_002, outcome_016, and outcome_005 consistency panels linked to H103. If these are consistent, validation of H103 or a stronger multi-outcome pattern would be justified; if they are discordant or subthreshold, the feature_048 lead should be closed. Meanwhile, existing active untested panels such as H20-H26, H65-H72, and H85-H90 remain useful for broad negative coverage. All conclusions are dataset-specific associational statements; causal interpretation and external generalizability remain unsupported.
